segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Spanish dialects don't change very much. Slang changes a lot,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: but Spanish is pretty standard. It's not like Arabic, for example, where you have such a different Arabic in Morocco to Egypt,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: for example. All of the different Spanishes are completely mutually intelligible,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: but in slang, you get many different terms and words, and car is one of these words that have different versions. Money is another one.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You might hear dinero, which is like the standard word. You might hear plata, which actually means silver.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Pasta, you might hear pasta, that's one. They use that in Spain. So, we had a few words for car. Do you remember any of them?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Um, máquina, auto, carro.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Carro.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Carro.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Two r's. Let's stay with carro. How would you say the car?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: El carro.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: El carro. And how would you say a car?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Un carro.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Un carro. Good. So it's a masculine word and we use el for the and un for a. What if we say the cars?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Los carros.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Los carros. So the plural of el is los. It's a little bit different, el to los.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word for expensive is caro. So it's like carro, but with one r. Caro.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Caro.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So again, it's a nice pair to feel the difference between having the single r and the double r just as we saw in pero meaning but and perro meaning dog.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say the car is expensive?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: El carro es caro.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. El carro es caro. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So es we said was it is, she is, he is, or just is, or you are talking to usted, talking formally.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if you just wanted to say it is expensive?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es caro.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And what if you were talking about a feminine thing?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es cara.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Es cara. And when I say feminine thing, I really mean a feminine noun. If you're referring in your mind to a feminine noun, because if you in your country call cars máquinas, then you're going to say es cara.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But if you call them autos, then you're going to say es caro. So it refers to the word more than the object, to the noun, the gender of the noun.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So es we have for is, and for they are or you guys are, we know they always come together, we have son, son, s-o-n.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Son.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Son. So if you want to say the cars are expensive, and we will use carro again. So the cars are expensive.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Los carros son caro... uh caros.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Los carros son caros. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What if you use a feminine word like máquina, how is it going to be, the cars are expensive?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Las máquinas son caras.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Las máquinas son caras. And the car is expensive using again máquina?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La máquina es caro... uh cara.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. La máquina es cara.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word teacher in Spanish is professor, profesor.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Profesor.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Profesor. So how would you say he is a professor? And we don't need to say a, we can just say he is professor.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es profesor.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Es profesor. What if you wanted to say she is a professor, what do you think might happen?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es profesora?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Es profesora. What if you wanted to say they are teachers and you mean a group of females?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Son profesoras.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Son profesoras. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So this is a noun, profesor. It's a word you can put the or a in front of. Now we said that adjectives, they change for gender if they end in -o. If they don't, they don't.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For example, the global situation was?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La global situación.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And where does that global go?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah, la situación global.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: La situación global. So situación is feminine, but we're not saying globala. Adjectives, these describing words that we can put is in front of,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: they only change if they end in -o. But nouns, they can change to feminine like profesor, profesora, to differentiate.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So this is why it's important to know what type of word we're dealing with. We're doing this already, but we don't even realize it. The moment we come in contact with a verb, we know exactly what to do.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We know it's a verb and we know how to manage it. We don't start trying to make a verb masculine or feminine, for example. So we're already making this differentiation, but we want to do it more consciously to get more control.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So this is a noun. Doctor, what do you think that means?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Doctor.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Is it a noun, is it an adjective, is it a verb, what is it?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Noun.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Noun. So how do you think feminine, a female doctor, would be?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Doctora.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, doctora. We just stick an a. Good. So how would you say he is a doctor?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es doctor.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. She is a doctor?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es doctora.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Now if you want to get the plural of professor, profesor, or doctor, doctor, or any other word in Spanish that ends in a consonant,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: you don't add -s, you add -es. So how do you think it would sound, the plural of profesor?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Profesores.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, profesores. So this is the plural for masculine or for mixed. The plural for feminine?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Profesoras.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So how would you say they are professors and you mean a masculine or mixed group?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Son profesores.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Son profesores. And if they were all female?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Son profesoras.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. They are doctors, mixed or masculine?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Son doctores.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Son doctores. What if they were females?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Son doctoras.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Son doctoras. Good. Words ending -ive in English, -i-v-e, tend to become -ivo, -i-v-o, for masculine singular.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This is the one we always start from now and build from. This masculine singular or neuter let's say. So for example, addictive becomes adictivo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now when I say neuter, we don't really have a neuter in Spanish. We have masculine and feminine, but the concept of neuter exists. Let's say, for example, if I say it's addictive and I'm referring

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: to living in the mountains is addictive, eating healthily is addictive, or something like this, then I use the masculine singular. So how would you say it's addictive?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es adictivo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Es adictivo. How would you say he is positive?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es positivo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And you pronounced an s, where most English speakers will probably find themselves pronouncing a z there because in English we have positive, positive. So that would probably transfer into Spanish to positivo, and we want to be careful not to do that, positivo with an s, positivo. She is positive?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es positiva.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. They are positive?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Son positivos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. They are intuitive?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Son intuitivos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Son intuitivos. What if you meant women?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Intuitivas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Son intuitivas. She is very attractive. The word for very is muy,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and it's spelled m-u-y. The y, you can imagine it like an i. Muy.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Muy.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So she is very attractive?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es muy atractivo. Oh, atractiva. So es muy atractiva.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Atractiva is showing us that it refers to a female, so this would probably help us work out who we're talking about, but maybe we would want to say it to clarify or to emphasize or to contrast.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say that using the word for she? She is very attractive.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I always get confused on that, if it's él or if it's la or ella.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So I want you to spend some time to think about it and not guess. Think about which is which and make a decision.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Her is la.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ella es muy atractiva.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Ella es muy atractiva. How would you say she is very creative?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ella es muy creativa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But she's aggressive?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Pero es... is it agresiva? I was thinking of the double g. Does it stay...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Well, these random double letters that we don't need in English, really, they just become single letters in Spanish. So I think there's a double s there as well in English. Well, that would also become single. The only double letters that cross over are the r's and the n's,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: like connotación.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah, double n's...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Connotación. If you get a double f, a double s, double g, these random double letters you get in English, they don't cross over into Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say they are aggressive talking about a masculine or a mixed group?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Son agresivos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And what if you wanted to use the word for they?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ellos son agresivos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How would you say he is negative?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es negativo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And if you use the word for he?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Él es negativo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. He's very negative.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es muy negativo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say it's intensive, it's intensive?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es intensivo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So we we use the neuter there, we don't know what we're talking about, so we can just use the masculine singular which is also like neuter: es intensivo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say they are natives? They are natives.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Son nativos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Son nativos. And what if it was a female group?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Son nativas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good.
